property_summary: For any caller who is the current owner, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) updates the contract's owner to newOwner; the mutant that comments out the assignment breaks this by leaving owner unchanged for some inputs.

For any address caller that is the current owner, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) always makes c.owner() equal newOwner afterwards; the mutant that omits the assignment can leave c.owner() unchanged for some fuzzed newOwner, violating this rule.

For any addresses ownerAddr and newOwner (with ownerAddr not equal to address(0)), if ownerAddr is the contract owner and calls transferOwnership(newOwner), then afterwards c.owner() == newOwner; the mutant that removes the assignment can leave c.owner() unchanged for some newOwner values and thus violates this rule.

For any nonzero address newOwner and when msg.sender is the current owner, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) results in c.owner() == newOwner; the mutant that omits the assignment can leave owner unchanged for some fuzzed newOwner, so the property detects that difference.

For any address newOwner and when the current owner calls transferOwnership(newOwner), the contract's owner() afterward equals newOwner; the mutant that removes the assignment can leave owner unchanged for some newOwner values, violating this rule.

For any address newOwner supplied by the caller and when called by the current owner, transferOwnership updates the contract's owner to exactly that newOwner; the mutant instead sets owner to address(0) for some inputs, breaking this rule.

For any caller who is the current owner and any _newOwner address, after transferOwnership(_newOwner) completes the contract's owner() getter equals the supplied _newOwner; the mutant that assigns msg.sender instead breaks this rule for inputs where msg.sender != _newOwner.

For any caller who is the current owner and any target address newOwner, after transferOwnership(newOwner) completes the contract's owner() equals newOwner; the mutant that sets owner = msg.sender instead will violate this whenever the caller (msg.sender) is different from newOwner.

For any current owner caller and any target _newOwner address, after transferOwnership(_newOwner) completes the contract's owner() equals the provided _newOwner (i.e., ownership is assigned to the argument, not to the caller); the mutant that sets owner = msg.sender will violate this whenever the caller (msg.sender) differs from the provided _newOwner.

For any address newOwner and any caller who is the current owner, after calling transferOwnership(newOwner) the contract's owner() equals the supplied newOwner; the mutant that assigns owner = msg.sender instead will break this when the caller (msg.sender) differs from newOwner.

For any address newOwner and any caller who is the current owner, after transferOwnership(newOwner) completes the contract's owner() equals the supplied newOwner; the mutant that assigns owner = msg.sender violates this rule whenever the caller (msg.sender) differs from newOwner.

For any caller who is the current owner, after calling transferOwnership(newOwner) the contract's owner equals the provided newOwner (the reference sets owner = _newOwner); the mutant that assigns tx.origin instead will violate this when msg.sender != tx.origin (e.g., when an owner calls through a proxy contract), so owner != _newOwner.

For any owner caller and any target newOwner address, when the current owner directly calls transferOwnership(newOwner) the contract's owner becomes the provided newOwner (reference: owner = _newOwner); the mutant that assigns owner = tx.origin can be distinguished by having the owner call through a proxy contract so msg.sender != tx.origin, which will make owner != newOwner.

For any addresses owner and newOwner and any proxy contract Proxy called by owner, when owner (the current owner) invokes transferOwnership(newOwner) directly (msg.sender == tx.origin) the contract's owner becomes newOwner; the mutant that assigns tx.origin breaks this rule when the call comes through a proxy (msg.sender != tx.origin) because owner becomes tx.origin instead of newOwner.

For any addresses a (initial owner) and delegate (a contract the owner uses to call through) and target (newOwner), if a is the current owner and a calls transferOwnership(target) through a deployed Proxy that forwards the call (so msg.sender != tx.origin), then the reference sets owner==target but the buggy mutant would set owner==tx.origin (breaking the rule).

If an owner calls transferOwnership(newOwner) directly (so msg.sender == tx.origin), the contract's owner becomes the provided newOwner; the mutant that assigns tx.origin instead would only differ when the call is proxied (msg.sender != tx.origin), so the rule is: for any owner and newOwner, when the current owner calls transferOwnership(newOwner) directly, c.owner() == newOwner (the buggy mutant can be made to violate this by causing msg.sender != tx.origin, but this property restricts to direct calls where reference and mutant behave the same — to detect the mutant we instead assert that when the owner calls through a proxy, the reference still sets owner==newOwner while the mutant will set owner==tx.origin), however to satisfy the requirement that the reference holds for ALL admissible inputs and the mutant breaks for SOME input, the test asserts that if the owner calls transferOwnership through a proxy contract (so msg.sender != tx.origin), then the reference still sets owner == newOwner — the mutant which assigns tx.origin will violate this for some fuzzed inputs.

For any caller who is the current owner and any target address newOwner, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) results in c.owner() == newOwner (the reference preserves the supplied new owner); the mutant that assigns a fixed constant address breaks this rule for inputs where newOwner != 0x000...1.

Invariant: after any call to transferOwnership(newOwner) performed by any caller, the contract's owner() remains unchanged unless the caller was the current owner — the reference enforces onlyOwner so only the current owner can change owner, while the mutant (removed require) allows non-owners to change owner and thus can violate this rule for some caller/newOwner inputs.

Invariant: Only the current owner can successfully call transferOwnership, so after any call to transferOwnership by an address A the owner becomes A iff A was the pre-call owner; the mutant inverts the check allowing non-owners to call transferOwnership and thus can change owner when a non-owner calls it, violating the invariant.

Invariant: calling owned() (which is onlyOwner) never changes the public owner variable — reference preserves owner across any caller, whereas the mutant assigns owner = msg.sender inside owned() and thus can change owner when called by the owner.

For any caller who is the current owner, invoking owned() does not change the public owner variable; the mutant assigns owner = msg.sender inside owned(), allowing owner to be (redundantly) re-written and thus potentially differing after the call.

For any caller addr, calling owned() when msg.sender == c.owner() leaves c.owner() unchanged (reference keeps owner identical before and after the call); the mutant assigns owner = msg.sender inside owned(), so when the owner calls owned() the state write still leaves the owner equal but the behavioral difference can be observed when owner is changed to a different address beforehand and then a non-owner calls owned() — the reference reverts due to onlyOwner, but the mutant also reverts; to expose difference we instead check that only the owner can successfully call owned() (call succeeds iff caller == owner) — reference enforces this for all callers, while the mutant still enforces it but additionally writes state when owner calls it, so we detect the mutant by observing that a call by the owner does not change owner in the reference but may in the mutant when owner is a contract that returns different msg.sender via delegatecall; however, to create a concrete distinguishing input, we use a helper contract that initially becomes owner via transferOwnership and then calls owned() — the reference preserves owner after the helper's call, but the mutant sets owner to the helper's internal tx-origin (msg.sender) which differs if the helper forwards calls, producing a differing owner; thus the property: after any caller who is a contract calls owned() (and the call succeeds), c.owner() remains equal to the caller's address (i.e., onlyOwner prevents others) and specifically for contract callers the owner remains the same address after the call — the mutant that assigns owner = msg.sender can change owner when the owner is a contract that performs a forwarding call, causing the post-call owner to differ.

For every caller address a, calling owned() succeeds iff a == c.owner(), and after a successful call by the owner the public owner value remains equal to the original owner (i.e. owned() does not change owner); the mutant breaks this by assigning owner = msg.sender inside owned(), so when the current owner (an EOA) calls owned() the public owner becomes the caller (same) — to distinguish we use a contract owner that forwards the call so msg.sender differs causing the mutant to change owner to the forwarder while the reference keeps owner equal to the contract owner address.

For any address caller that successfully invokes owned() (i.e. caller == c.owner()), the public owner stored in c must remain equal to the caller afterwards; the mutant that assigns owner = msg.sender inside owned() can change c.owner() when the caller is a contract that forwards the call (so msg.sender inside C differs from the contract's address), violating this property.

The reference contract guarantees that calling owned() does not change owner unless the caller is the current owner (onlyOwner enforces msg.sender == owner); the mutant removes that check allowing non-owners to change owner via owned(), so there exists a caller address for which owner differs after calling owned().

For all callers, calling owned() does not change C.owner (only the owner can invoke owner-only effects); the mutant removes the require check allowing some caller to change owner via owned(), violating this invariant.

For every caller address, invoking owned() does not change C.owner (only the current owner can execute owner-only actions); the mutant removes the require in onlyOwner so some caller can change the owner via owned(), violating this rule.

For any caller address A, calling owned() must revert unless A == c.owner() (only the owner may call owner-only functions); the mutant removes the require so some non-owner caller will succeed calling owned(), violating this rule.

For every caller address, calling owned() must only succeed when msg.sender == owner (i.e., only the owner can call owned()); the mutant inverts the check so some non-owner callers can call owned(), breaking this rule for some fuzzed caller addresses.

For any caller who is the current owner, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) always updates C.owner to newOwner; the mutant that removes the assignment breaks this by leaving owner unchanged for some newOwner inputs.
